'''Jamie Whyte''' is a New Zealand [[classical-liberal]] academic and politician who was the Leader of [[ACT New Zealand]] in 2014. He unsuccessfully contested the [[Pakuranga (New Zealand electorate)|Pakuranga electorate]] in the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 general election]].<ref>{{cite news | url= http://www.nzherald.co.nz/election-2014/news/article.cfm?c_id=1503581&objectid=11195810 | title=Act leader set to play it straight | work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] | date=3 February 2014 | access-date=3 February 2014 | author=Young, Audrey}}</ref> At the election, Whyte held the first position on the party list, but ACT did not achieve enough party votes to secure any list seats.<ref name="JamieWhyte">Act. [http://www.act.org.nz/jamie-whyte "Jamie Whyte"] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20140917134019/http://www.act.org.nz/jamie-whyte |date=17 September 2014 }}, ''[[Act New Zealand]]'', 27 October 2005. Retrieved on 18 September 2014.</ref> Soon after the 2014 general election, he resigned from the leadership of ACT.<ref name="Whyte resigns">{{cite news | url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/10576531/ACTs-Jamie-Whyte-quits-as-leader | title=ACT's Jamie Whyte quits as leader | work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] | date=3 October 2014 | access-date=3 October 2014}}</ref>

Whyte is a former philosophy lecturer, currency trader and management consultant. He has written books and newspaper columns about reasoning and politics.

== Early life and academia ==
Whyte was born in [[Auckland]], New Zealand. He received his undergraduate degree from the [[University of Auckland]].<ref>{{cite news | url= http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11195695 | title=Jamie Whyte elected Act leader | work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] | date=2 February 2014 | access-date=18 September 2014 | author=Young, Audrey}}</ref> He then moved to the UK to study for an M.Phil and Ph.D at [[St John's College, Cambridge]].{{citation needed|date=June 2017}}

Upon graduation, Whyte remained at Cambridge University for three years as a research fellow at [[Corpus Christi College, Cambridge|Corpus Christi College]] and temporarily lectured in the philosophy faculty and at the University of Reading. He won the ''Analysis'' journal prize for the best article by a philosopher under the age of 30.<ref>{{Cite journal|url = https://philosophynow.org/issues/101/News_March_April_2014|title = Philosopher becomes party leader|last = Roberts|first = Sue|date = March 2014|journal = Philosophy Now|access-date = 18 September 2014}}</ref>

==Early career==
Whyte then took up a job with the New York-based management consultancy firm [[Oliver Wyman]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.lse.ac.uk/publicEvents/events/2011/20110726t1830vOT.aspx|title=Keynes v Hayek |date= 8 August 2011| publisher=London School of Economics}}
</ref> He also worked as a foreign currency trader.{{citation needed|date=June 2017}}

==Writing and media==
Since 2003, Whyte has written books for general audiences and newspaper columns, aiming to expose shoddy reasoning, especially by politicians. In 2006 he won the [[Reason Foundation]] Bastiat Prize for journalism (jointly with Tim Harford of the ''[[Financial Times]]'') and in 2010 he was named runner-up.<ref>Previous Bastiat Prize Winners from [http://reason.org/news/show/1012830.html Reason Foundation], accessed June 2014.</ref> In June 2014, Whyte won the [[Institute of Economic Affairs]]' Arthur Seldon Memorial Award for Excellence for ''Quack Policy''.<ref>{{Cite news|url = http://www.iea.org.uk/in-the-media/press-release/political-party-leader-wins-prestigious-seldon-award|title = Political party leader wins prestigious Seldon Award|date = 27 June 2014|access-date = 18 Sep 2014|publisher = IEA}}</ref>

Whyte is the author of ''Crimes Against Logic'' (titled ''Bad Thoughts: A Guide to Clear Thinking'' in the UK; 2003), ''A Load of Blair'' (2005), ''Free Thoughts'' (2012) and ''Quack Policy'' (2013). He has also written columns for many notable publications, including ''[[The Times]]'', [[City A.M.|City A.M]]., [[Standpoint (magazine)|Standpoint]], ''Financial Times'' and ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]''.{{citation needed|date=June 2017}}

Whyte has also occasionally broadcast on [[BBC Radio 4]] and television.{{citation needed|date=June 2017}}

== Political career ==
In his youth, Whyte was a campaign volunteer for [[Bob Jones (businessman)|Bob Jones]]' [[New Zealand Party]] in the [[1984 New Zealand general election|1984 general election]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11283858|title=Leaders' first trip to ballot box|author=Cherie Howie|publisher=[[New Zealand Herald]] |date=2014-06-29}}</ref>

Despite no prior experience in political office, Whyte was elected to the ACT party's leadership at a board meeting in February 2014, beating former MP, [[John Boscawen]]. At the same meeting, [[David Seymour]] was chosen as ACT's candidate for the [[Epsom (New Zealand electorate)|Epsom electorate]]<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.3news.co.nz/ACT-choices-huge-risk-for-party/tabid/1607/articleID/330702/Default.aspx|title= ACT choices huge risk for party|author= Sabin|date= 2 February 2014|publisher= 3 News|first= Brook|access-date= 2 February 2014|archive-date= 3 February 2014|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140203235416/http://www.3news.co.nz/ACT-choices-huge-risk-for-party/tabid/1607/articleID/330702/Default.aspx|url-status= dead}}</ref>; Kenneth Wang was elected as Whyte's deputy leader in April 2014.<ref>{{Cite news|url = http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/9944101/Kenneth-Wang-elected-Act-deputy-leader|title = Kenneth Wang elected Act deputy leader|last = Dastgheib|first = Shabnam|date = 15 April 2014|access-date = 18 Sep 2014|publisher = Stuff.co.nz}}</ref>

During his tenure as leader, Whyte drew controversy when he stated his opinion that incestuous relationships between consenting adults should not be illegal.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-29 |title=Incest comment defended |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/act-leader-jamie-whyte-stands-by-incest-comments/IWFUOHB7LNIDQ7GSW6DFVJRDO4/ |access-date=2023-08-28 |website=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |language=en-NZ}}</ref>

In the 2014 general election, ACT only won enough votes to be represented by David Seymour in the [[Epsom (New Zealand electorate)|Epsom electorate]]. After the election, on 3 October 2014 Whyte resigned from the leadership of the party, saying: "Clearly, I make this announcement with regret, however the election result is clear, and I must now turn to my career and my family." He was replaced as ACT leader by Seymour on the day of his resignation.<ref name="Whyte resigns"/>

In February 2017, Whyte joined the [[Institute of Economic Affairs]] as Director of Research.<ref>{{cite web|title=IEA appoints new Director of Research & a new Chief Economist|url=https://iea.org.uk/media/institute-of-economic-affairs-unveils-major-new-appointments/|access-date=20 February 2017}}</ref> He left the think tank on 1 January 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://twitter.com/_JamieWhyte/status/1078332999375163393|title=I am leaving the IEA as of 1 Jan 2019. I will miss it. But I won't miss the endless "who funds you?" tweets. They reveal a profound misunderstanding of the kind of people who work at think tanks and what motivates them. And always irrelevant to the issue at hand. So stupid.|first=Jamie|last=Whyte|date=27 December 2018}}</ref>

Whyte's political philosophy is [[classical liberalism]], in the tradition of [[Friedrich Hayek]].<ref>Hayek vs Keynes at the LSE (Cobden Centre), accessed June 2014.</ref>
